QF.id: IV Fixed Income Instruments and Bond Markets_50

question.text: A dynamic bond fund manager observes an inverted yield curve and forms a view that long-term yields will fall over the coming months as the curve normalizes. To benefit most from this view, the manager should:

answer.text: Increase allocation to long-duration / long-term bonds
Shift the entire portfolio to equity
Increase allocation to short-term instruments only
Ignore the rate view and keep the portfolio unchanged

explanation.text: The Logic: Bond prices move inversely to yields, and the price impact is amplified by duration (pp.68 and 161 of the workbook). If the manager explicitly expects long-term yields to fall, the position that captures the biggest price gain is a long-duration / long-maturity bond allocation (option A). The yield-curve discussion on pp.31-34 supports this rate view as one path by which an inverted curve normalizes. The Trap: Option B abandons the rate view entirely and changes asset class. Option C reduces duration and forgoes the price gain. Option D ignores the view. In the original ambiguous version the stem merely said the manager observes an inverted curve and "considers curve normalization" without committing to a long-rate-fall view. Curve normalization can occur via short rates falling, long rates rising, or both - so a long-duration position is not uniquely supported without an explicit long-yield-fall view. Note: The original question was ambiguous because curve normalization has multiple paths and the stem did not specify which. The stem has been tightened to include the explicit "long-term yields will fall" view, so option A (long-duration positioning) is uniquely correct. Source: NISM Series IV, Dec 2025, pp.31-34, 68, 161.
